picks.title: Shapes on a Quilt
picks.skill: Name and count shapes
picks.skillEs: nombrar y contar formas
picks.directions: Look at the picture of the quilt. Plan, then record your answer.
picks.prompt: Tell what shapes you see on the quilt. How many of each shape are there?

picture.alt: A colorful quilt made of nine squares in three rows. Four squares have a red triangle, three squares have a yellow circle, and two squares have a blue rectangle.

vocab.meaning: a shape with 3 sides
a round shape
a shape with 4 sides and 4 square corners

models.A: I see triangles and circles.
models.B: I see four red triangles and three yellow circles. There are two blue rectangles too.
models.C: The quilt has nine squares in three rows. I counted four red triangles, which is the most. There are three yellow circles and only two blue rectangles. Altogether, that is nine shapes, one in each square, because four plus three plus two equals nine.

picks.hint: Touch each triangle and count out loud. Then do the circles.
picks.extension: Tell which shape there is the most of and how you know.

picks.title: Classroom Jobs
picks.skill: Describe and explain a job
picks.skillEs: describir y explicar un trabajo en el salón
picks.directions: Look at the picture of the classroom. Plan, then record your answer.
picks.prompt: Tell what jobs the students are doing. Which job do you want?

picture.alt: A classroom where students do jobs. A boy feeds the fish in a fish tank, a girl waters a plant by the window, and another boy hands out papers at two desks. The teacher sits at her desk.

vocab.meaning: a task someone does to help
give food to
give one to each person

models.A: A boy feeds the fish.
models.B: A boy is feeding the fish, and a girl is watering the plant. I want to hand out papers because I like to help.
models.C: In this classroom, every student has a job. One boy is feeding the fish in the fish tank. A girl is watering the plant by the window, and another boy is handing out papers at the desks. I would like the fish job because I love animals. Also, the fish need food every day, so it is an important job.

picks.hint: Name one job first. Then say: I want to ___.
picks.extension: Tell about a job you do at home.

picks.title: Shopping at the Market
picks.skill: Say what you like and why
picks.skillEs: decir qué les gusta y por qué
picks.directions: Look at the picture of the market. Plan, then record your answer.
picks.prompt: What would you buy at this market? Tell why.

picture.alt: An outdoor community market with three stands. The fruit stand sells apples for 50¢ each and bananas. The vegetable stand sells corn for 25¢ each and carrots. The bread stand sells loaves of bread for $2 each. A seller stands behind each stand. A mother and her son buy apples, and a man carries a shopping bag.

vocab.meaning: a place where people sell food and other things
pay money to get something
a small table or shop at a market

models.A: I want apples.
models.B: I would buy apples because they are sweet. I like bananas too.
models.C: If I went to this market, I would buy apples from the fruit stand. One reason is that apples are sweet and crunchy, and they are healthy for me. Also, they only cost 50 cents each, so I could buy one for my brother too. After that, I would get bread for my family's dinner.

picks.hint: Point to a food you like. Say: I like ___ because it is ___.
picks.extension: Tell what your family likes to buy at the store.

picks.title: A Visit to the Library
picks.skill: Describe a place and what people do there
picks.skillEs: describir un lugar y lo que hace la gente allí
picks.directions: Look at the picture of the library. Plan, then record your answer.
picks.prompt: Tell about the library. What do you see? What are the people doing?

picture.alt: A library with tall bookshelves full of books. A boy reads a book on a green beanbag chair. At the front desk, a librarian helps a girl check out a book. A plant sits on a small table.

vocab.meaning: a place where you can borrow books
the person who helps you find books
take a book home for a short time

models.A: I see books. A boy reads.
models.B: I see shelves with a lot of books. A boy is reading on a green beanbag, and a girl is checking out a book.
models.C: This picture shows a quiet library with tall shelves full of books. A boy is reading on a comfy green beanbag chair. At the front desk, the librarian is helping a girl check out a book. I think the girl is happy because she can take her book home. There is also a plant on a small table.

picks.hint: Start with the place: I see a library. Then tell about one person.
picks.extension: Tell what kind of book you would check out and why.

picks.title: What Do You See at Recess?
picks.skill: Describe people and actions in a picture
picks.skillEs: describir a las personas y lo que hacen en una imagen
picks.directions: Look at the picture of the playground. Plan, then record your answer.
picks.prompt: Tell what you see on the playground. Who is there? What are they doing?

picture.alt: A busy playground with a tall slide, two swings, a tree, and a basketball hoop. Five kids wait in a long line for the slide. One girl swings, and the other swing is empty. Two boys play with a ball near the hoop. A teacher stands by the tree.

vocab.meaning: a tall toy you climb up and slide down
a seat that hangs and moves back and forth
people standing one behind the other

models.A: I see kids. They are on the slide.
models.B: I see five kids in a line for the slide. A girl is on the swing, and two boys play with a ball.
models.C: I see a busy playground at recess. First, there are five kids waiting in a long line for the slide. Next to them, a girl is swinging, but the other swing is empty. Two boys are playing with a ball near the basketball hoop. A teacher stands by the tree, so everyone is safe.

picks.hint: Point to one person. Say who it is and what the person is doing: A girl is swinging.
picks.extension: Tell which place on the playground you would go to first and why.

picks.title: Dinner Together
picks.skill: Describe a scene and connect it to your life
picks.skillEs: describir una escena y relacionarla con su vida
picks.directions: Look at the picture of the family dinner. Plan, then record your answer.
picks.prompt: Describe what this family is doing. Then tell about dinner at your home.

picture.alt: A family eats dinner together at a table. A grandmother passes a bowl of rice, a father pours water, and two children smile. There is a plate of chicken, a salad, and a basket of bread on the table. A lamp hangs over the table.

vocab.meaning: the people you live with or are related to
hand something to another person
something a family does again and again

models.A: They eat. We eat rice.
models.B: In the picture, the grandmother is passing rice, and the father is pouring water. At my house, we eat dinner together too, and we have rice and beans.
models.C: In the picture, a family is eating dinner together at a big table. The grandmother is passing a bowl of rice, the father is pouring water, and the two children are smiling. They have chicken, salad, and bread. At my house, we also eat together on Sundays. My abuela makes pupusas, and that is my favorite dinner because we cook them together.

sayFor: who is at the table and what they are doing
one thing about your own family
picks.hint: Tell about the picture first. Then start a new sentence with At my house …
picks.extension: Ask a partner about their family's favorite dinner.

picks.title: Take Care of the Garden
picks.skill: Explain steps to care for plants
picks.skillEs: explicar los pasos para cuidar las plantas
picks.directions: Look at the picture of the school garden. Plan, then explain your steps.
picks.prompt: A new class will take care of this garden. Explain the steps they should follow.

picture.alt: A school garden with two wooden garden beds. Tomato plants grow in one bed, and tall sunflowers grow in the other bed. A girl waters the tomatoes with a watering can, and a boy digs with a small shovel. The school building is behind the garden.

vocab.meaning: a plant that grows where you do not want it
a tool for digging
strong and growing well

models.A: Water the plants.
models.B: First, you should water the tomatoes and sunflowers. Then dig out the weeds because they take the water. Finally, pick the red tomatoes.
models.C: Taking care of the garden takes a few steps. First, water the tomatoes and sunflowers with the watering can, because plants need water every day. Next, use the small shovel to dig out weeds, so they do not take water from the plants. After that, check for ripe red tomatoes and pick them carefully. Finally, put the tools away so the garden stays neat.

sayFor: garden jobs: water, dig, pull weeds
picks.hint: Look at what the kids are doing in the picture. Each action is a step.
picks.extension: Explain what the garden needs in the winter.

picks.title: Lemonade Math
picks.skill: Explain how to solve a math problem
picks.skillEs: explicar cómo resolver un problema de matemáticas
picks.directions: Look at the picture of the lemonade stand. Plan, then explain your thinking.
picks.prompt: Amir wants to buy 3 cups of lemonade. Explain how to find how much money he needs.

picture.alt: Two kids at a lemonade stand. A sign on the stand says Lemonade 50¢ a cup. A girl stands behind the stand with a pitcher of lemonade and a stack of cups. A boy in front of the stand holds coins in his hand.

frames: I can ___ to find the total.

vocab.meaning: how much money you pay
small units of money; 100 cents make 1 dollar
add the same number many times

models.A: Three cups. One dollar fifty.
models.B: One cup costs 50 cents. I add 50 plus 50 plus 50, and that is 150 cents. So Amir needs one dollar and fifty cents.
models.C: The sign says one cup of lemonade costs 50 cents. Amir wants three cups, so I can multiply 3 times 50. That equals 150 cents. Since 100 cents is one dollar, 150 cents is the same as one dollar and fifty cents. So Amir needs $1.50 to buy three cups.

picks.hint: Find the price on the sign first. Then count by 50s three times.
picks.extension: How many cups could Amir buy with $2.00? Explain.

picks.title: A Morning at the Market
picks.skill: Describe a scene with details
picks.skillEs: describir una escena con detalles
picks.directions: Look at the picture of the community market. Plan, then record your answer.
picks.prompt: Describe the market. Tell what each stand sells and what the people are doing.

picture.alt: An outdoor community market with three stands. The fruit stand sells apples for 50¢ each and bananas. The vegetable stand sells corn for 25¢ each and carrots. The bread stand sells loaves of bread for $2 each. A seller stands behind each stand. A mother and her son buy apples, and a man carries a shopping bag.

frames: The mother and her son are ___.

vocab.meaning: the people and places in the area where you live
a person who sells things
how much money something costs

models.A: There is fruit and bread.
models.B: The market has three stands. One stand sells apples and bananas, and the next one sells corn and carrots. A mother and her son are buying apples.
models.C: This picture shows a busy community market with three stands. The fruit stand sells apples for 50 cents and bananas too. Next to it, the vegetable stand has corn and carrots, and the bread stand sells loaves for two dollars. A mother and her son are buying apples, while a man walks by with a shopping bag. It looks like a friendly place where neighbors shop together.

sayFor: the three stands and what they sell
connecting words: and, also, next to
picks.hint: Go from left to right: first stand, next stand, last stand.
picks.extension: Tell about a market or store in your neighborhood.

picks.title: Sort the Recycling
picks.skill: Explain how and why to recycle
picks.skillEs: explicar cómo y por qué reciclar
picks.directions: Look at the picture of the students recycling. Plan, then record your answer.
picks.prompt: Explain how the students should sort the things on the table. Why is recycling important?

picture.alt: Two students sort recycling at school. There are three bins labeled Paper, Plastic, and Cans. A boy puts a plastic bottle in the Plastic bin, and a girl holds a newspaper. A table next to them has a cardboard box, a can, and another bottle waiting to be sorted.

vocab.meaning: use old things to make new things
a big container
thick, strong paper used to make boxes

models.A: Bottle in plastic.
models.B: The box goes in the paper bin, and the can goes in the cans bin. The bottle goes in the plastic bin. Recycling is good because it makes less trash.
models.C: The students need to put each thing in the right bin. First, the cardboard box goes in the Paper bin, because cardboard is made of paper. Next, the can goes in the Cans bin, and the bottle goes in the Plastic bin. Recycling is important because old things can become new things. As a result, there is less trash in the land and ocean.

sayFor: which bin each thing goes in
picks.hint: Name one thing on the table. Then name the bin with the same kind of material.
picks.extension: Explain one way your family can make less trash.

picks.title: Plan Field Day
picks.skill: Compare conditions and make a recommendation
picks.skillEs: comparar condiciones y hacer una recomendación
picks.directions: Look at the two weather pictures. Plan, then record your recommendation.
picks.prompt: Your school must choose a day for outdoor field day. Compare the weather in the two pictures and recommend which day is better. Explain what students should bring.

picture.alt: Two weather scenes. On the left, the sun shines in a blue sky and a boy in a T-shirt and shorts flies a kite. On the right, dark clouds drop rain, and a girl in a yellow raincoat and boots holds an umbrella next to a puddle.

frames: On the sunny day, ___, while on the rainy day, ___.

vocab.meaning: say what you think is the best choice
what the weather will probably be
tell how things are alike and different

models.A: The sunny day is better.
models.B: The sunny day is better for field day because kids can run and play outside. On the rainy day, the grass is wet and kids need umbrellas. Students should bring water.
models.C: On the sunny day, the sky is clear and a boy can even fly a kite, while on the rainy day, dark clouds drop rain and make puddles. I recommend the sunny day for field day because students can run races safely on dry grass. On the other hand, the rainy day could make the field slippery and dangerous. Students should bring water bottles and hats so that they stay cool in the sun.

sayFor: compare the two kinds of weather
compare words: while, but, on the other hand
picks.hint: Tell one thing about each picture. Then pick one and say why.
picks.extension: Suggest an indoor activity for the rainy day.

picks.title: The Ice Cube Race
picks.skill: Explain an experiment, its result, and the reason
picks.skillEs: explicar un experimento, su resultado y la razón
picks.directions: Look at the picture of the ice experiment. Plan, then record your explanation.
picks.prompt: Explain what happened in this experiment and why. What does it show about heat?

picture.alt: A science experiment outside. Two plates each started with three ice cubes. The plate in the sunshine now has only a puddle of water. The plate in the shade under a tree still has three small ice cubes. A boy writes notes on a clipboard.

frames: The ice in the sun ___, while the ice in the shade ___.

vocab.meaning: change from solid to liquid when it gets warm
a cool, dark place out of the sun
how hot or cold something is

models.A: The ice in the sun melted.
models.B: The boy put ice on two plates. The ice in the sun melted into water, but the ice in the shade did not melt because it was cooler.
models.C: In this experiment, a boy put three ice cubes on each of two plates. He placed one plate in the sunshine and the other in the shade under a tree. After a while, the ice in the sun melted into a puddle, while the ice in the shade was still there. This happened because the sun heats things up and raises the temperature. Therefore, the experiment shows that heat makes ice melt faster.

sayFor: the cause: heat from the sun
picks.hint: Organize it: what he did → what happened → why → what it shows.
picks.extension: Predict what would happen to a chocolate bar in the sun. Explain.

picks.title: The Life Cycle of a Plant
picks.skill: Explain a cycle with academic vocabulary
picks.skillEs: explicar un ciclo con vocabulario académico
picks.directions: Look at the four pictures of the pots. Plan, then explain the plant's life cycle.
picks.prompt: Explain the life cycle of a flowering plant. Tell what happens at each stage and what the plant needs.

picture.alt: Four pots in a row show how a plant grows. First, a seed is planted in the soil and watered. Next, a small sprout with two leaves comes up. Then, the plant grows taller with more leaves in the sun. Last, a yellow flower opens.

frames: The plant needs ___ in order to ___.

vocab.meaning: when a seed starts to grow
one step in a cycle
steps that happen again and again in a circle

models.A: A seed grows into a flower.
models.B: First, the seed is planted and gets water, and then it germinates into a sprout. Next, the plant grows taller with more leaves. Finally, it makes a flower.
models.C: The life cycle of a plant begins when a seed is planted in soil and watered. During the next stage, the seed germinates and a small sprout with two leaves pushes up. Then the stem grows taller and makes more leaves, because the plant uses sunlight and water to make food. In the last stage, a flower opens, and later the flower makes new seeds. That is how the cycle starts all over again.

sayFor: science words: germinate, roots, stem, flower
picks.hint: Use one science word for each picture: seed, germinate, stem, flower.
picks.extension: Compare the plant life cycle to the life cycle of a butterfly.

picks.title: The Lost Dog, Told Your Way
picks.skill: Narrate with details, feelings, and dialogue
picks.skillEs: contar una historia con detalles, sentimientos y diálogo
picks.directions: Look at the three pictures. Plan, then tell the whole story.
picks.prompt: Tell the story as if you were the girl. Include what happened, how you felt, and something a character said.

picture.alt: A picture story in three parts. 1: A brown dog runs out of an open gate while a girl waters flowers. 2: The girl and her father put a Lost Dog poster on a tree. 3: A neighbor brings the dog back, and the girl hugs her dog.

vocab.meaning: afraid something bad might happen
happy because a problem is over
the words characters say

models.A: My dog ran away. I was sad.
models.B: One day, my dog Canela ran out of the gate while I watered the flowers. I felt worried, so my dad and I made a poster. Then our neighbor brought her back.
models.C: One sunny afternoon, I was watering my flowers when I noticed the gate was open. Suddenly, my dog Canela ran out and disappeared down the street! I felt so worried that I started to cry. My dad said, "Let's make a poster so our neighbors can help." The next day, Mr. Haddad knocked on our door holding Canela, and I hugged her tight. I felt relieved, and now I always close the gate.

picks.hint: Tell it with I and my. Add one feeling for each picture.
picks.extension: Tell the same story from the dog's point of view.

picks.title: Why Communities Need Markets
picks.skill: Explain how a place helps a community
picks.skillEs: explicar cómo un lugar ayuda a la comunidad
picks.directions: Look at the picture of the market. Plan, then record your answer.
picks.prompt: Explain how a market like this one helps a community. Use details from the picture and give at least two ways.

picture.alt: An outdoor community market with three stands. The fruit stand sells apples for 50¢ each and bananas. The vegetable stand sells corn for 25¢ each and carrots. The bread stand sells loaves of bread for $2 each. A seller stands behind each stand. A mother and her son buy apples, and a man carries a shopping bag.

frames: A market helps a community because ___.

vocab.meaning: a person who grows or makes things to sell
a person who buys things
things people make or grow to sell

models.A: People buy food there.
models.B: A market helps a community because people can buy fresh food like apples and corn. Also, the sellers make money for their families.
models.C: A market helps a community in several ways. First, consumers can buy fresh goods close to home. For example, the mother and her son are buying apples, and a man is carrying a full shopping bag. Second, the producers earn money when they sell their fruit, vegetables, and bread, so they can support their families. Overall, a market brings neighbors together and keeps money in the community.

picks.hint: Think about two groups: the people who buy and the people who sell.
picks.extension: Explain how another place, like a library or a fire station, helps a community.

picks.title: What Is the Weather?
picks.skill: Describe weather and clothing
picks.skillEs: describir el clima y la ropa
picks.directions: Look at the picture. Write about the weather. Tell what the boy is wearing.
picks.prompt: Look at the picture. What is the weather like? What is the boy wearing?

picture.alt: A rainy day: gray clouds, falling rain, and a boy in a yellow raincoat and boots holding a blue umbrella next to a puddle.

vocab.meaning: what it is like outside, like rain or sun
a cover you hold over you in the rain
a jacket that keeps rain off

models.A: It is rainy. The boy has an umbrella.
models.B: It is a rainy day, and the sky is gray. The boy is wearing a yellow raincoat and boots. He holds a blue umbrella because he wants to stay dry.
models.C: Today the weather is cold, gray, and very rainy. Dark clouds cover the sky, and rain is falling everywhere. Because of the rain, the boy is wearing a yellow raincoat and rubber boots. He also holds a big blue umbrella over his head. He is ready to splash in the puddle and still stay dry.

picks.hint: What falls from the clouds? What keeps the boy dry?
picks.extension: Write what the boy should NOT wear today and why.

picks.title: Write About the Shapes
picks.skill: Describe shapes with numbers and colors
picks.skillEs: describir formas con números y colores
picks.directions: Look at the picture of the shapes. Write how many of each shape you see. Use number words and color words.
picks.prompt: Look at the picture of the shapes. How many circles, triangles, and squares do you see?

picture.alt: Shapes on a table: three red circles, two blue triangles, and one yellow square.

vocab.meaning: a round shape
a shape with three sides
a shape with four equal sides

models.A: I see three red circles. I see one square.
models.B: I see three red circles on the table. There are two blue triangles too. There is only one yellow square, so there are six shapes in all.
models.C: There are six shapes on the table, and they come in three colors. First, I count three red circles in a row at the top. Next to them are two blue triangles with three sides each. Below the circles, there is one yellow square. There are more circles than any other shape.

picks.hint: Count each shape. One shape = is. More than one = are, and add -s.
picks.extension: Write one more sentence: How many shapes are there in all?

picks.title: Pick a Class Pet
picks.skill: Give an opinion with a reason
picks.skillEs: dar una opinión con una razón
picks.directions: Look at the two pictures. Which class pet is better, the fish or the hamster? Write your choice and one reason.
picks.prompt: Look at the two pictures. Which pet should our class get? Why?

picture.alt: Two choices for a class pet: a goldfish in a fish tank and a hamster in a cage with a wheel.

vocab.meaning: an animal that lives with people
more good than the other one
a word that tells why

models.A: I like the fish. It is pretty.
models.B: I think our class should get the hamster. I like it because it is soft and fun to watch. It runs on the wheel, so it is never boring.
models.C: Our class should get a goldfish as a class pet. First, a fish is quiet, so it will not bother us when we read or take tests. Also, it only needs a little food each day and a clean tank. A hamster is cute, but it can bite and needs more care. For these reasons, a goldfish is the best pet for our classroom.

picks.hint: First pick one pet. Then finish: because it is ___.
picks.extension: Add a second reason with also.

picks.title: Write About the Park
picks.skill: Describe a picture with simple sentences
picks.skillEs: describir una imagen con oraciones sencillas
picks.directions: Look at the picture of the park. Write 1 or 2 sentences. Tell what you see and what the children are doing. You can write on paper too.
picks.prompt: Look at the picture of the park. What do you see? What are the children doing?

picture.alt: A sunny park with a tree, a girl on a swing, a boy kicking a red ball, a brown dog, and a bench.

vocab.meaning: an outdoor place with grass, trees, and things to play on
a seat on ropes or chains that moves back and forth
to hit something with your foot

models.A: I see a park. A girl is on the swing.
models.B: A girl swings beside a tree. A boy kicks a red ball.
models.C: Beside the tree, a girl is swinging while a boy kicks a red ball nearby.

sayFor: tells what one person is doing (is + -ing)
a capital letter and a period
picks.hint: Point to one person. What is that person doing? Write: The ___ is ___ing.
picks.extension: Add a color word: The boy is kicking a red ball.

picks.title: How to Make a Sandwich
picks.skill: Explain steps in order
picks.skillEs: explicar los pasos en orden
picks.directions: Look at the pictures. Write how to make a sandwich. Write one sentence for each step.
picks.prompt: Look at the pictures. How do you make a sandwich? Write the steps.

picture.alt: Three steps to make a sandwich: 1) two slices of bread on a plate, 2) cheese and lettuce on one slice, 3) the finished sandwich cut in half.

vocab.meaning: one part of how you do something
a thin, flat piece
to place something somewhere

models.A: Put bread on a plate. Put cheese on the bread.
models.B: First, put two slices of bread on a plate. Then put cheese and lettuce on one slice. Last, put the bread on top and cut the sandwich in half so it is easy to eat.
models.C: Making a sandwich is easy if you follow three steps. First, place two slices of bread side by side on a clean plate. Next, add a slice of cheese and some green lettuce to one piece of bread. Finally, put the other slice on top and cut the sandwich in half. Now your lunch is ready to share or eat.

sayFor: the food words from the pictures
picks.hint: Start each step with an action word: Put, Add, Cut.
picks.extension: Add one more step: what do you do after you make it?

picks.title: Describe the Community Market
picks.skill: Describe a community place with details
picks.skillEs: describir un lugar de la comunidad con detalles
picks.directions: Look at the picture. Write 3–4 sentences that describe the community market. Tell what people sell and what people do.
picks.prompt: Look at the picture of the market. What do the stands sell? What are the people doing?

picture.alt: A busy community market with two stands under striped roofs, one selling fruit and one selling vegetables, a seller, and a mother and child carrying a shopping bag.

frames: One stand sells ___, and the other sells ___.

vocab.meaning: a place where people buy and sell things
a person who sells things
a person who buys things

models.A: I see a market. They sell fruit.
models.B: The community market is busy today. One stand sells apples, oranges, and bananas, and the other stand sells carrots and lettuce. A mother and her child are shopping because they need food for dinner.
models.C: On a sunny day, the community market is full of fresh food. On the left, a friendly seller stands behind a table of red apples, oranges, and bananas. Next to it, a stand with a green striped roof sells carrots, lettuce, and tomatoes. Meanwhile, a mother and her child carry a shopping bag full of vegetables. Markets like this help families buy fresh food close to home.

picks.hint: Start with the stands: what is on each one? Then write about the people.
picks.extension: Tell why markets are important for a community.

picks.title: Picture Story: The Lost Backpack
picks.skill: Narrate a story with time words and feelings
picks.skillEs: contar una historia con palabras de tiempo y sentimientos
picks.directions: Look at the three pictures. Write a story of 3–4 sentences. Tell what happens in each picture and how the characters feel.
picks.prompt: Look at the three pictures. What happens to the green backpack? Write the story.

picture.alt: Three panels: 1) a boy walks away from a school bus and leaves his green backpack on the seat, 2) a girl on the bus finds the green backpack, 3) the girl gives the backpack back to the boy at school and they both smile.

vocab.meaning: to not remember something
to see something you were looking for
to give something back

models.A: The boy left his backpack. The girl gave it back.
models.B: First, a boy got off the bus, but he forgot his green backpack. Then, a girl on the bus found it on the seat. At the end, she gave it back to him at school, and he was happy because his homework was inside.
models.C: One morning, Daniel learned how much a kind friend can help. First, he jumped off the school bus in a hurry and left his green backpack on the seat. Soon after, Amina saw the backpack and picked it up carefully. When she got to school, she ran to the door and handed it to Daniel. He smiled and said thank you, because all of his homework was safe.

sayFor: what happens in all three pictures
time words: first, then, at the end
picks.hint: Write one sentence for each picture, then add a feeling sentence.
picks.extension: Give the characters names and add something they say.

picks.directions: A class grew bean plants. Plant A got 2 spoons of water a day and grew 14 centimeters in two weeks. Plant B got 6 spoons a day and grew 9 centimeters. Write a paragraph that makes a claim and supports it with data.
picks.prompt: What can you say about the amount of water and plant growth? Write a paragraph with a claim, evidence, and reasoning.

vocab.meaning: a statement that answers a question
facts from data that support a claim
the explanation of how the evidence supports the claim

models.A: Plant A grew taller than Plant B. Plant A grew 14 centimeters.
models.B: My claim is that Plant A, with less water, grew taller. The data show that Plant A grew 14 centimeters and Plant B grew 9 centimeters.
models.C: My claim is that more water did not help the bean plant grow taller in this test. The data show that Plant A, with 2 spoons a day, grew 14 centimeters, while Plant B, with 6 spoons a day, grew only 9 centimeters. This shows that too much water may slow growth, because the roots may not get enough air. More trials would help us be sure.

sayFor: a claim that answers the question
numbers from the data as evidence
reasoning with because or this shows

picks.extension: Add one more sentence with a detail, a reason, or a transition word.

Another reason is that more students would enjoy books if they had comfortable seats. Thank you for thinking about my idea. Sincerely, Sam

picture.alt: Two hillsides next to a river after a rainstorm. The left hillside is covered with trees and grass, and the river beside it is blue and clear. The right hillside has only tree stumps and bare brown soil, with deep grooves where mud has washed down into the river, turning that part of the river brown.

vocab.meaning: when water or wind wears away and carries off soil or rock

models.A: One side has trees. One side has no trees. The mud goes in the river. Trees are good.
models.B: The left hillside has trees and grass, but the right hillside only has stumps. When it rained, the right side lost a lot of soil. This happened because there were no roots to hold the soil. As a result, mud went into the river and made it brown. The left side stayed the same because the trees protected it.
models.C: The picture compares two hillsides after the same storm, and the main difference is that the trees on the right side were cut down. On the left, tree roots and grass hold the soil in place, so the rain soaked in and the river stayed clear. On the right, however, nothing protected the bare soil, so the rushing water carved deep grooves and carried mud downhill. As a result, the river next to that hillside turned brown with sediment, which could harm fish and plants. This shows that cutting down trees can cause erosion and pollute nearby water.

sayFor: what you see on each hillside
picks.hint: Ask yourself: What is different between the two sides BEFORE the rain? That difference is the cause.
picks.extension: Suggest one way people could protect the right hillside from more erosion.

picks.title: Explain: How a Homemade Water Filter Works
picks.skill: Explaining a process from a diagram
picks.skillEs: explicar un proceso a partir de un diagrama

picks.prompt: Using the diagram, explain step by step how the water filter cleans muddy water.

picture.alt: A diagram of a cut plastic bottle turned upside down as a water filter. Muddy brown water is poured in at the top. It passes down through a layer of gravel, then a layer of sand, then a layer of black charcoal, then a cotton pad, and clear water drips into a glass at the bottom.

frames: First, the water ___, where the ___ traps ___.

vocab.meaning: something that lets liquid pass through but stops solid pieces

models.B: First, you pour muddy water into the top. Next, the water goes through the gravel, which stops big pieces. Then it goes through the sand, which stops small dirt. After that, the charcoal cleans it more. Finally, cleaner water comes out into the glass.
models.C: This diagram shows how a homemade filter cleans muddy water in four stages. First, the water is poured into the top of the bottle, where the gravel traps large particles such as leaves and pebbles. Next, the water seeps through the sand, and because the spaces between sand grains are tiny, smaller bits of dirt get stuck. Then the water passes through activated charcoal, which absorbs some chemicals and odors. Finally, the cotton pad catches the last fine particles, so clearer water drips into the glass. However, this filter does not kill germs, so the water would still need to be boiled before anyone could drink it.

picks.hint: Move top to bottom. For each layer, say what it is AND what it does: "The sand traps ___ because ___."

picks.title: Respond to a Counterclaim: Community Service Hours

frames: I understand that ___, and that concern is valid.

vocab.meaning: an argument against your claim
an answer that shows why the other argument is weaker
fair and reasonable

models.A: I don't agree. Service is good. You help people. It is only 10 hours.
models.B: I understand that students are busy with homework and sports. However, I think community service should be required. It is only 10 hours in a whole year. For example, you could help at a food bank on two Saturdays. Helping the community teaches responsibility.
models.C: I understand my classmate's point that many students already balance homework, sports, and responsibilities at home, and that concern is valid. However, I disagree that this is a reason to drop the requirement. Ten hours spread over a school year is less than twenty minutes a week, which most students could manage. In addition, service can fit into what students already do; for example, a student who babysits siblings could volunteer with them at a library reading event. Ultimately, the requirement builds skills and connections that students carry into high school, so the benefits outweigh the small amount of time it takes.

sayFor: a respectful restatement of the other view
picks.hint: Begin by showing you listened: "I understand that ___." Then turn with "However, ___."
picks.extension: Suggest a compromise that would address your classmate's concern.

picks.title: Summarize Aloud: Why Cities Are Hotter
picks.skill: Summarizing an informational text orally
picks.skillEs: resumir en voz alta un texto informativo

picks.prompt: Summarize the article "Urban Heat Islands" in your own words.

vocab.meaning: related to a city
the dark, hard material used to build roads
to bounce light or heat back

models.A: Cities are hot. Roads are dark. Not many trees. They paint roofs white.
models.B: The article is about why cities are hotter than the countryside. One reason is that dark roads and roofs take in heat. Another reason is that cities have fewer trees. To fix this, some cities paint roofs white and plant trees.
models.C: The article explains that cities, which scientists call urban heat islands, can be up to 7 degrees hotter than nearby rural areas. This happens mainly because dark asphalt and roofs absorb heat during the day and release it at night, and because cities have fewer trees to provide shade. As a result, people use more electricity, and heat waves become dangerous for children and older adults. To solve the problem, some cities are painting roofs white to reflect sunlight and planting trees in the hottest neighborhoods first.

sayFor: the main idea in one sentence
your own words, not copied sentences
picks.hint: Paraphrase: say the idea a new way. Change "absorb sunlight" to "soak up heat from the sun."
picks.extension: Which solution would work best in your neighborhood? Give one reason.

picks.title: Summarize a Short Story: The Broken Bridge

picks.skillEs: resumir con sus propias palabras los sucesos principales de un cuento
picks.directions: Read the short story. Then summarize it aloud in 4-5 sentences without reading it word for word. Tell who the story is about, the problem, the main events in order, and how it ends. Leave out the small details.
picks.prompt: Story: Every morning, Dani walked across a wooden footbridge to reach school. One stormy night, the river rose and broke the bridge in two. The next day, the town said it would take a year to build a new one. Dani did not want to wait. He asked his neighbors for help, and together they gathered logs and rope. After two weekends of hard work, they built a small bridge. It was not beautiful, but it was strong enough. When Dani crossed it on Monday, his neighbors cheered. He realized that a problem feels smaller when many people share the work. Summarize this story.
frames: In summary, the story shows that ___.

vocab.meaning: to tell the most important parts of a text in fewer words
strong and not easily broken
working together to reach a goal

models.A: Dani walks to school on a bridge. The bridge breaks. The neighbors help. They make a new bridge. Dani is happy.
models.B: This story is about a boy named Dani. His bridge to school broke in a storm, and the town said a new one would take a year. Dani asked his neighbors for help, and they built a small bridge in two weekends. In the end, Dani learned that a problem is easier when people work together.
models.C: The story is about a boy named Dani, whose footbridge to school was destroyed in a storm. Although the town said a replacement would take a year, Dani refused to wait, so he persuaded his neighbors to help him. Together, they spent two weekends gathering materials and building a small but sturdy bridge. As a result, Dani could cross the river again, and his neighbors cheered. In summary, the story shows that cooperation can solve a problem faster than waiting for someone else to fix it.

sayFor: the main events in order, not every detail
how the problem is solved or what the character learns
your own words, not copied sentences
picks.hint: Ask yourself four questions: Who? What was the problem? What did they do? How did it end? Answer each in one sentence.
picks.extension: Summarize the story again in only two sentences, keeping the problem and the solution.

picks.skillEs: escribir un pie de foto que explique una imagen
picks.directions: Look at the picture. Write a caption (1–2 sentences) that tells what is happening.
picks.prompt: Write a caption for this science class picture.

picture.alt: A scientist looks into a microscope. Test tubes stand in a rack on the table.

vocab.meaning: words that explain a picture
to watch carefully
a science test

models.A: Use the word bank: student, microscope, experiment, observe, learn.

picks.hint: A caption tells WHO is doing WHAT.
picks.extension: Add why the student is doing the experiment.

picks.title: Write: Describe a Picture
picks.skill: Writing 2–3 descriptive sentences with frames
picks.skillEs: escribir de 2 a 3 oraciones descriptivas con frases de apoyo
picks.directions: Look at the picture. Write 2–3 sentences to describe it. Use the frames and word bank.
picks.prompt: Describe what you see near the school.

picture.alt: A school building with trees in front and a crosswalk on the street.

vocab.meaning: lines where people cross the street
close to
to tell what something is like

models.A: Use the word bank: school, tree, crosswalk, students, near.

picks.hint: Name two things you see and tell where they are.
picks.extension: Add one color word to one of your sentences.

picks.title: My Morning Routine
picks.skill: Sequencing with time words
picks.skillEs: ordenar sucesos con palabras de tiempo
picks.directions: Write three short sentences about your morning. Use first, then, and last.
picks.prompt: What do you do in the morning before school? Write three sentences in order.

vocab.meaning: things you do the same way each day
the thing you do at the start
the thing you do at the end

models.A: Use the frame "First, I ___." Then start the next sentence with "Then."

picks.hint: Begin each sentence with a time word: First, Then, Last.
picks.extension: Add what time you do one of these things.

picks.title: Write: My Favorite Subject
picks.skill: Writing a short opinion with one reason
picks.skillEs: escribir una opinión corta con una razón
picks.directions: Write 2–3 sentences about your favorite subject. Give ONE reason using 'because.'
picks.prompt: What is your favorite subject, and why?

vocab.meaning: the one you like best
a school class like math or science
why you think something

models.A: Use the word bank: favorite, subject, because, learn, fun.

picks.hint: Name the subject, then add 'because' and a reason.
picks.extension: Add a second sentence about what you do in that class.

picks.title: Explain a Bar Graph
picks.skill: Describing data in writing
picks.skillEs: describir datos por escrito
picks.directions: Imagine a class survey. Write 3-4 sentences that explain what the data shows. Use comparison words.
picks.prompt: Our class voted for favorite lunch: pizza got 14 votes, tacos got 9, and salad got 4. Explain what the data shows.

vocab.meaning: facts or numbers you collect
to show how things differ
chosen by many people

models.A: Start with "The data shows that ___." Then compare two choices using "more than."

picks.hint: Use words like "most," "fewer than," and "the least" to compare the numbers.
picks.extension: Predict what might change if the class voted again next month.

picks.title: Summarize a Short Text
picks.skill: Writing a brief summary
picks.skillEs: escribir un resumen breve
picks.directions: Read the short text in your head, then write a 3-4 sentence summary in your own words.
picks.prompt: Summarize: "Recycling turns used items into new products. It saves energy and keeps trash out of landfills. Many cities now collect paper, plastic, and glass at the curb." Write a summary.

vocab.meaning: a short retelling of the main points
making used items into new ones
a place where trash is buried

models.A: Begin with "This text is mainly about ___." Then add one benefit the author gives.

picks.hint: A summary states the main idea first, then one or two key details. Do not copy the text exactly.
picks.extension: Add one opinion sentence telling whether you think recycling is worth it.

picks.title: Write: Compare Two Choices
picks.skill: Writing a comparison with transition words
picks.skillEs: escribir una comparación con palabras de transición
picks.directions: Compare two after-school activities. Write 4–6 sentences. Tell how they are alike and different, then choose one.
picks.prompt: Compare joining the soccer team and joining the art club. How are they alike and different? Which would you choose, and why?

vocab.meaning: tell how things are alike
tell how things are different
a word that shows a difference

models.A: Use compare/contrast words: both, alike, however, while, on the other hand.

picks.hint: Start with one similarity, then two differences, then your choice.
picks.extension: Add one sentence about who would enjoy each activity.

picks.title: Write: Explain with Evidence
picks.skill: Writing an explanation supported by evidence
picks.skillEs: escribir una explicación apoyada con evidencia
picks.directions: Write 4–6 connected sentences. Make a claim and support it with evidence using 'because,' 'but,' and 'so.'
picks.prompt: Should our school start a garden club? Make a claim and support it with at least two reasons.

vocab.meaning: a statement you support
facts that support a claim
a word that shows contrast

models.A: Use expansion words: because (reason), for example (evidence), but (contrast), so (result).

picks.hint: Claim → reason → example → address an objection → conclusion.
picks.extension: Add a specific number or fact as evidence.

picks.title: Write: Persuade Your Principal
picks.skill: Writing a short persuasive message to an audience
picks.skillEs: escribir un mensaje corto para convencer a un público
picks.directions: Write a short message (5–6 sentences) to persuade the principal. State your request, give two reasons, and end politely.
picks.prompt: Write to your principal asking for more time in the library each week. Give two reasons and a polite ending.
frames: Dear Principal ___, I am writing because ___.

vocab.meaning: to convince someone to agree
something you politely ask for
polite and considerate

models.A: Use persuasive language: I am writing because, first/second, for these reasons, thank you.

picks.hint: Greeting → request → reason 1 → reason 2 → polite closing.
picks.extension: Add a sentence that answers a possible 'no' from the principal.

picks.title: Explain: Why Do We Have Seasons?
picks.skill: Writing an explanatory paragraph from a diagram
picks.skillEs: escribir un párrafo explicativo a partir de un diagrama
picks.directions: Look at the diagram of Earth orbiting the Sun. Write an explanatory paragraph (5-7 sentences) that explains why the Northern Hemisphere has summer and winter.
picks.prompt: Explain why the Northern Hemisphere has summer in June and winter in December. Use the diagram and precise science vocabulary.

picture.alt: A diagram of the Sun in the center with Earth shown at two places in its orbit. On the left, Earth's tilted axis leans its northern half toward the Sun, and sunlight hits the north directly. On the right, on the opposite side of the orbit, the same tilt now leans the northern half away from the Sun, and sunlight hits the north at a low slant.

frames: In June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted ___, so ___.

vocab.meaning: an imaginary line that Earth spins around
the path a planet travels around the Sun
one half of Earth

models.A: Earth goes around the Sun. Earth is tilted. In summer it is close. In winter it is far.
models.B: We have seasons because Earth is tilted. In June, the top of Earth leans toward the Sun, so it gets more sunlight and it is summer. In December, the top of Earth leans away from the Sun, so it gets less sunlight and it is winter. The tilt stays the same all year.
models.C: Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees as it orbits the Sun. In June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, so sunlight strikes it more directly and days are longer. As a result, the ground and air absorb more energy, and it is summer. Six months later, in December, Earth is on the opposite side of its orbit, and the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun. Sunlight hits it at a low angle and spreads out, and days are shorter, so it is winter. Many people think seasons are caused by Earth's distance from the Sun, but it is actually the tilt that matters.

sayFor: a topic sentence that names the cause (Earth's tilt)
a concluding sentence that corrects a common mistake
picks.hint: Distance is NOT the reason for seasons. Focus on the tilt: which half leans toward the Sun in each month?
picks.extension: Add a sentence explaining what season Australia has in June, and why.

picks.title: Phones at Lunch: Make an Argument
picks.skill: Writing a claim with evidence
picks.skillEs: escribir una afirmación con evidencia
picks.directions: Write a short paragraph (4-6 sentences) that states a claim and supports it with two reasons.
picks.prompt: Should students be allowed to use phones during lunch? State your claim and support it with two reasons.

vocab.meaning: the position you argue for
why your claim is true
the sentence that wraps up your idea

models.A: Use the structure: claim, reason one, reason two, example, conclusion.

picks.hint: Start with your claim, give two reasons, add an example, and finish with a conclusion sentence.
picks.extension: Add one sentence that answers a person who disagrees with you.

picks.title: Bus or Walking: Compare Ways to School
picks.skill: Writing a compare-and-contrast response
picks.skillEs: escribir una respuesta que compare y contraste
picks.directions: Write a paragraph comparing two ways to get to school. Explain which is better and why.
picks.prompt: Compare riding the bus and walking to school. Which is better and why? Write 4-6 sentences.

vocab.meaning: to show how things are alike
to show how things are different
considering everything together

models.A: Use "Both ___" to show similarity and "However" or "In contrast" to show difference.

picks.hint: Show one way they are alike and two ways they are different, then state which is better.
picks.extension: Add a sentence about which choice is better in bad weather.

picks.title: Write a Narrative: When the Lights Went Out
picks.skill: Developing a narrative with sequence, dialogue, and detail
picks.skillEs: desarrollar una narración con orden, diálogo y detalles
picks.directions: Read the opening of a story. Then continue the story in your own words.
picks.prompt: Opening: "When the lights went out in the middle of the school play, Ana froze on stage." Write 7-9 sentences that continue the story. Show what happens next in order, include one line of dialogue, describe what Ana sees, hears, or feels, and end by showing how the problem was solved.

vocab.meaning: words that characters say, written inside quotation marks
the order in which events happen
the way the problem in a story is solved

models.A: Ana froze on the stage. It was dark. She heard people talking. Her friend said, "Keep going." Ana said her lines. The lights came on, and everyone clapped.
models.B: When the lights went out, Ana froze on stage. She heard the audience whisper in the dark. Then her friend Leo whispered, "Keep going, you know your lines." Ana took a deep breath and spoke. A few seconds later, the lights came back on, and everyone clapped. Ana felt proud.
models.C: The dark stage suddenly felt enormous, and Ana could hear the audience murmuring and chairs creaking. Her heart pounded so loudly that she forgot her next line. At that moment, her friend Leo leaned close and whispered, "Just say it the way we practiced." Ana closed her eyes, took a slow breath, and began to speak, her voice shaking at first and then growing steadier. A few seconds later, the lights flickered back on, and the audience burst into applause. Although her hands were still trembling, Ana smiled, because she had learned that she could keep going even when everything went wrong.

sayFor: events in a clear order with time words
one line of dialogue with quotation marks
details about what Ana sees, hears, or feels
a closing sentence that shows what Ana learned
picks.hint: Plan the moment in three parts: what Ana feels, who helps her, and how the lights come back. Add one sound and one feeling.
picks.extension: Add a sentence at the end that tells how Ana acts differently the next time something goes wrong.

picks.title: Compare and Contrast: Athens and Sparta
picks.skill: Writing a compare-and-contrast paragraph from a table
picks.skillEs: escribir un párrafo que compare y contraste a partir de una tabla
picks.directions: Both Athens and Sparta were city-states in ancient Greece. Use the information in the table to write a compare-and-contrast paragraph.
picks.prompt: Write a paragraph of 6-8 sentences about how Athens and Sparta were alike and how they were different. Compare at least two topics from the table, and end with a sentence that explains what the differences show.

vocab.meaning: a city with its own government and land
a person who has rights and duties in a city or country
strict training and self-control

models.A: Athens and Sparta were both Greek cities. In Athens, men voted. In Sparta, kings led the city. Boys in Sparta trained to be soldiers.
models.B: Athens and Sparta were both city-states in ancient Greece, but they were different. In Athens, male citizens voted on laws, but in Sparta two kings led the city. Boys in Athens studied music and public speaking. Boys in Sparta left home at age 7 to train as soldiers.
models.C: Athens and Sparta were both powerful city-states in ancient Greece, yet they valued very different things. In Athens, male citizens voted on laws in an assembly, whereas Sparta was led by two kings and a small council. Both cities educated boys, but the goals were not the same: many Athenian boys studied reading, music, and public speaking, while Spartan boys left home at age 7 to train as soldiers. Unlike Athens, which honored art, philosophy, and trade, Sparta treated discipline and military strength as most important. These differences show that two cities in the same civilization can build very different ways of life.

sayFor: a topic sentence that introduces both city-states
at least two topics compared, such as government, education, or values
comparison words (both, similarly, whereas, in contrast)
a concluding sentence about what the differences show
picks.hint: Read across each row of the table so you compare the SAME topic for both cities before you move on to the next topic.
picks.extension: Add a sentence that predicts how a Spartan boy and an Athenian boy might each describe a good citizen.
